SEC14A-01.note: Inverted order: subject is 'two silver pennies' (plural), far after the verb; 1911 narrative needs past. A (singular, pulled by 'slab') is the strong trap. C/D present tense can be struck from the past-tense frame alone.

SEC14A-02.note: Head noun 'practice' is singular; sentence needs a finite main verb. A/B are non-finite (fragment). C 'have' agrees with 'sources'/'editors' inside the long relative clause - strongest distractor.

SEC14A-03.note: Colon after an independent clause introduces the list of four noun phrases; 'four separate pieces of' telegraphs it. B semicolon needs an independent clause after; C makes a fragment; D 'which the' is garbled and strikable on sight.

SEC14A-04.note: Correlative 'so high a multiple ... that' takes no punctuation before 'that'; the 'so' is far back. D 'so that' duplicates 'so' but reads naturally - strongest. A is struck by the common 'no comma before that' heuristic.

SEC14A-05.note: 'Whatever he wrote ..., if anything,' is a noun-clause subject of 'has seldom survived', so a new sentence is required. A is a comma splice that reads as a free relative tacked onto 'cue' - strong. C adds 'that' and is struck on form.

SEC14A-06.note: 'facing' is non-finite, so 'the boards ... facing' cannot be a clause; only the participial phrase 'leaving the boards ... facing' works. A, C, D each create a subject with no finite verb (fragment). D 'whereupon' is the most tempting.

SEC14B-01.note: Subject is the noun clause 'Whether those spores survive ... truffles' (singular); 'since the 1980s' demands present perfect. A 'have kept' agrees with adjacent plural 'truffles' - strong. B/D wrong tense with 'since'.

SEC14B-02.convention: Informal object 'who' is widely tolerated but not in the SAT's formal convention; counted exclusive on that basis
SEC14B-02.note: Two axes: 'whom' is the object of 'considered'; the belief ended with the 1998 find ('until'), so simple past, not present perfect. C (whom + have) is the strongest distractor; D right tense, wrong case.

SEC14B-03.note: Dangling modifier: 'Bleached nearly white ...' must modify the lichen, so the lichen must be the subject. A's possessive 'the lichen's first collector' is the trap (subject is still the collector). B/C open with a person.

SEC14B-04.note: Two independent clauses; semicolon, with 'after sunset' fronted in the second. A comma splice; C attaches 'after sunset' to the wrong clause (contradicting the sense) and still splices; D 'which the' garbled, strikable on form.

SEC14B-05.note: Introductory 'While' clause needs a comma before the main clause; without it 'cools a seed crystal' garden-paths as transitive (B, strongest). C leaves 'While ... cools.' a fragment; D pairs subordinator with 'and'.

SEC14B-06.note: Appositive 'a cyanobacterium whose cells ... plankton,' sits between the subject and 'accounts'; 'cells measure' needs a relative 'whose' to stay inside it. D comma splices inside the appositive - strongest. A/B break subject from verb; the lone word-adding option is the key.

tells: Added-connector options are almost never the key: 03D 'which', 04D 'so that', 05C 'that', 06C 'although', 06D 'whereupon', B04D 'which', B05C 'Then', B05D 'and' are all wrong. Exception: B06C 'whose' (key) and 06B 'leaving' (key, but a participle not a connector). A test-taker using 'reject the option that adds a conjunction/relative' strikes one distractor on 03, 04, 05, B04, B05 and two on 06.
'which the' garbled distractor template recurs verbatim in 03D and B04D; free strike in both.
B06: the only option that is not a bare punctuation mark is the key (odd-one-out by form).

No mark family is uniformly key or non-key: period key in 05 only (wrong 03, 06, B05, B06); semicolon key in B04 (wrong 03, B06); colon key in 03 (wrong 04); no punctuation key in 04 (wrong 05, B05). Letter distribution of my answers is 3/3/3/3.
near_duplicates: SEC14A-02 and SEC14B-01: same template - singular head (noun phrase / noun clause) separated from the verb by a plural noun, options are have/has-style pairs, key is the singular 'has ...'.
SEC14A-01 also agreement-across-distance (inverted), third agreement item in 12.
SEC14A-05 and SEC14B-04: both join two independent clauses where the second opens with a fronted element (noun clause / 'after sunset'); comma-splice distractor in both.
SEC14A-03 and SEC14B-04 share the 'X, which the' distractor.

phase2_note: All 12 keys match cold answers; no disputes; every explanation's distractor rejections are true. No drops. Caveats (not drop-worthy): A-03 grades easy, below a hard-route commission; A-02/B-01 share one template (consider shipping only one per form); batch-level 'added connector is never the key' tell and B-06 lone-word-option tell stand.
